processing: Sold as raw pu-erh, which normally means sun-dried maocha that is kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: Not documented for this mountain; across Xishuangbanna the spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: Typical of sun-dried Yunnan leaf: dark-green twisted strands with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: In young tea, typically clear pale gold.
appearance_wet: Typically olive-green whole leaves when young.
taste_profile: Little is documented about this mountain's flavour. Its neighbour Gedeng is described as honeyed and wildflower-scented with a quickly fading bitterness, which is a comparison and not a tasting note for this tea.

brewing.notes: The usual young sheng approach: rinse once, keep early steeps short, and judge the tea from there.

vintage_note: As with sheng pu-erh generally, it is sold by harvest year, young or with some age. Few teas carry this name, so check what the wrapper actually claims. One product uses the same name for Nannuo in Menghai, a different mountain.
description:
Kongming Mountain stands in Xiangming, in Mengla County, among the old tea mountains. Gedeng lies on one side and Mangzhi on another, and tea forest runs between them. It is better known for its scenery, with a flat summit, grassland, sea of cloud and limestone rainforest, than for its tea.

A small amount of raw pu-erh is sold under the name. Very little is documented about how it is grown or made, so assume ordinary sheng methods until a maker tells you otherwise.

For the cup, the nearest guide is its neighbours in Xiangming, not any settled description of this mountain. Brew it as young sheng and take your own notes.

Be careful with claims on the label. One product page calls it the highest of the six ancient tea mountains, but it is not on the usual list of six, and another treats Kongming Mountain as a name for Nannuo.
history: The mountain's name recalls Kongming, the courtesy name of Zhuge Liang. Legend has him sowing tea seed here, and the same kind of story is told on other Yunnan mountains; it is folklore, not record. Xiangming township draws part of its name from this mountain. Beyond that, little is documented about tea here, and no reliable date for its gardens is known.
